title: Entra Roles, Custom Roles, and Administrative Unit Scoping
body:
Microsoft Entra ID ships with over a hundred built-in roles covering everything from tenant-wide roles like Global Administrator down to narrow, service-specific roles like Exchange Administrator or Teams Administrator. Each built-in role bundles a fixed set of permissions (actions) that can't be edited; if a built-in role grants too much or too little, the alternative is a custom role, which is assembled from a subset of the permissions that Microsoft currently exposes for custom-role use (not every built-in-role permission is available to custom roles yet).

What makes role assignment genuinely flexible is administrative units (AUs) — containers that scope a role assignment to a specific slice of the directory, such as a region's users or a particular department's devices. Both built-in and custom roles can be assigned at AU scope, with one condition for custom roles: the custom role must include at least one permission relevant to users, groups, or devices, since those are the object types AUs can bound. This is what lets an organization stand up a regional helpdesk admin who can reset passwords only for users in their own AU, without granting anything close to tenant-wide User Administrator rights.

For the exam, the practical distinction to remember is that role definitions (what a role can do) and role scope (where it can do it) are separate concerns — a Consultant-level admin plans both independently, picking the least-privileged role definition and then narrowing its blast radius with an AU when a tenant-wide assignment would be overkill.

title: Custom Security Attributes vs. Directory Extensions
body:
Custom security attributes are business-defined key-value pairs that an admin can attach to Microsoft Entra users and enterprise applications (service principals) — nothing else, notably not groups or devices. Each attribute definition lives inside an attribute set (a named grouping used to delegate management), and supports one of three data types (Boolean, integer, string), can allow single or multiple values, and can restrict input to a predefined list of values or leave it free-form. A tenant can have up to 500 active attribute definitions and 500 attribute sets, and an individual object can carry up to 50 assigned attribute values.

The feature exists to solve a specific gap: ordinary directory extension attributes are readable by anyone who can already read the object, which makes them unsuitable for sensitive classification data (e.g., a cost center used to gate access to a storage container). Custom security attributes flip that default — read and write access is locked down through their own dedicated RBAC roles (Attribute Definition Administrator/Reader to manage the schema, Attribute Assignment Administrator/Reader to assign values), and critically, even Global Administrator has no access to them by default. That isolation is what makes them usable as the input to Azure attribute-based access control (ABAC) conditions, where an attribute value can gate access to specific Azure Storage blobs or other Azure resources.

For the exam, the key contrast to hold onto is: directory extensions are for storing arbitrary app data that anyone with object-read access can see, while custom security attributes are for authorization-relevant data that needs its own locked-down permission model, separate from the standard Entra admin roles.

title: External Collaboration Settings vs. Cross-Tenant Access Settings
body:
Microsoft Entra External ID actually splits governance of guest access into two distinct, complementary settings surfaces, and mixing them up is a common source of confusion. External collaboration settings are the tenant-wide guardrails for B2B collaboration in general — who inside the org is allowed to invite guests, whether guest self-service sign-up is permitted, and domain allow/block lists for who can be invited. These settings apply regardless of whether the external party even has a Microsoft Entra tenant of their own (e.g., a social identity or a personal email address).

Cross-tenant access settings, by contrast, specifically govern collaboration between two Microsoft Entra organizations, and they operate as a pair of independent inbound and outbound configurations. Outbound settings control whether your own users can access resources in an external Entra org; inbound settings control whether users from an external org can reach your resources. A default configuration applies to every external org you haven't explicitly configured, but organization-specific overrides take precedence — useful when a trusted partner needs broader access than the default policy allows. Cross-tenant access settings also carry trust settings, letting the resource tenant accept MFA and device-compliance claims a guest already satisfied in their home tenant, which avoids forcing them to re-prove those signals.

The automatic redemption setting is a smaller but exam-relevant detail: when both the home tenant (outbound) and resource tenant (inbound) enable it for the same relationship, an invited guest skips the consent prompt and invitation email entirely — a nuance in how B2B guest onboarding behaves across cross-tenant sync, manual invitations, and B2B direct connect.

title: Cross-Tenant Synchronization: Automated B2B Lifecycle
body:
Cross-tenant synchronization automates the create/update/delete lifecycle of B2B guest users between Microsoft Entra tenants that belong to the same organization — think a company with a central IT tenant and several regional or subsidiary tenants that all need frictionless access to shared apps. It's built on the same provisioning engine Entra uses for SaaS app provisioning, which makes the configuration experience (scoping filters, attribute mappings, transformations) familiar to anyone who has set up automatic user provisioning for a third-party app before.

Architecturally, it's a one-way push from a source tenant into a target tenant, and it only synchronizes internal member accounts from the source — it cannot pull external guests from the source tenant, which prevents accidental chained/looped synchronization. Configuration is split across both tenants: the target tenant must first opt in via its cross-tenant access settings (enabling inbound synchronization and, typically, automatic redemption so guests aren't emailed an invitation), and then the source tenant defines the actual sync job — who's in scope, which attributes flow, and what transformations apply. Both users and security groups can be synced, though nested groups and non-security group types aren't supported.

The lifecycle payoff is the real selling point for the exam: when a user is removed from scope in the source tenant — deleted, unassigned from the sync config, or moved out of an in-scope group — cross-tenant sync automatically soft-deletes the corresponding B2B account in the target tenant, closing a gap that manual B2B invitations leave wide open (a departed employee's guest accounts in partner tenants don't clean themselves up).

title: Microsoft Entra Connect Sync vs. Cloud Sync
body:
Both Microsoft Entra Connect Sync and Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync solve the same core problem — keeping on-premises Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID in sync — but with fundamentally different architectures. Entra Connect Sync runs a full synchronization engine on a Windows Server, backed by a local SQL database, and does the heavy lifting of matching, filtering, and transforming identities entirely on-premises. Cloud Sync flips that model: a lightweight provisioning agent installed on-premises acts purely as a bridge, while all the actual orchestration, scheduling, and rules processing happens in the Microsoft cloud, communicating over the same outbound-only connection technology used by Application Proxy and pass-through authentication.

That architectural shift unlocks capabilities that were painful or impossible with the on-premises engine — most notably native support for multiple disconnected Active Directory forests syncing into a single Entra tenant (valuable after a merger/acquisition, or in an org that never consolidated its forests), and built-in high availability through multiple active agents with automatic failover, rather than the single-server-plus-staging-mode pattern Connect Sync relies on. Cloud Sync configuration also lives entirely in the Entra admin center, so admins can manage and troubleshoot it without VPNing into an on-prem sync server.

The trade-off, as of this writing, is feature parity: organizations that depend on capabilities like device writeback, full password writeback in every scenario, Exchange hybrid attribute writeback, or heavily customized attribute-flow rules may still need Connect Sync, though Microsoft has been explicit that Cloud Sync is its strategic direction for new hybrid identity deployments and is actively closing those gaps.

title: Choosing a Hybrid Authentication Method
body:
Microsoft Entra hybrid identity solutions boil down to three authentication choices, and the choice is independent of which sync engine (Connect Sync or Cloud Sync) an org uses. Password hash synchronization (PHS) is the simplest: a hash of each user's on-premises password hash is synced to Entra ID every two minutes, and Entra ID itself validates sign-ins — no additional servers, no inbound firewall exceptions, and it's a prerequisite for several premium features (Entra ID Protection's leaked-credential detection, Entra Domain Services) regardless of which primary method an org ultimately picks. Pass-through authentication (PTA) keeps password validation on-premises: lightweight agents relay the credential check directly to on-prem AD in real time, so account-disabled, locked-out, or expired-password states are enforced instantly rather than waiting for a sync cycle — the trade-off is needing outbound-only agents (three recommended, for redundancy) with network access to domain controllers. Federated authentication hands sign-in off entirely to an external system like AD FS, useful for orgs with existing federation investments or third-party MFA requirements that Entra can't natively satisfy, at the cost of the most on-premises infrastructure to build and maintain (a load-balanced federation farm plus a perimeter-network proxy tier).

Seamless single sign-on (SSO) is an orthogonal add-on, not a fourth authentication method — it layers onto either PHS or PTA (not federation, which has its own SSO behavior) to eliminate unnecessary credential prompts for domain-joined devices already signed into the corporate network, without requiring Entra-joined or hybrid-joined devices to get that benefit.

Microsoft's stated recommendation, regardless of which primary method is chosen, is to also enable password hash sync as a backup — the real-world justification cited is that organizations hit by on-premises outages (ransomware being the common case) that already had PHS running were able to fail over to it and keep using cloud apps within hours, while organizations without it were locked out of even email for weeks until on-prem infrastructure was rebuilt.

title: Modern Authentication Methods: TAP, CBA, and Passkeys
body:
Microsoft Entra ID's authentication methods policy covers a wide surface, but three methods matter disproportionately for the SC-300 exam because of how they get used operationally rather than just as sign-in options. A Temporary Access Pass (TAP) is a time-limited passcode an admin issues to a user, configurable for single or multiple uses, whose entire purpose is bootstrapping — it lets a user authenticate once, without a password, specifically so they can then register a real passwordless method (like a passkey or Windows Hello for Business) or recover access after losing every other credential. It's a primary-authentication method, but it's meant to be short-lived by design.

Certificate-based authentication (CBA) lets Entra ID validate a user's identity directly against an X.509 client certificate rather than a password, and it can serve as a full primary authentication method as well as satisfying MFA when combined with another factor. Because it doesn't depend on a shared secret the user types in, it's grouped with Windows Hello for Business and FIDO2 as one of the phishing-resistant methods Microsoft explicitly recommends over SMS or authenticator push notifications, which remain vulnerable to real-time social-engineering relay attacks.

Passkeys (FIDO2) — including passkeys stored in Microsoft Authenticator as well as hardware security keys — round out that phishing-resistant tier: they're built on public-key cryptography where the private key never leaves the device/authenticator, so there's no shared secret for an attacker to phish or replay in the first place. For the exam, the useful mental model is a spectrum from weakest to strongest: password alone, then password plus a traditional MFA factor (SMS/voice/authenticator push, all phishable), then the phishing-resistant tier (CBA, FIDO2 passkeys, Windows Hello for Business) — and knowing that TAP's job is specifically to get a user from zero credentials onto that stronger tier, not to be a long-term sign-in method itself.

title: SSPR Registration Requirements and On-Premises Writeback
body:
Self-service password reset (SSPR) lets users unlock or reset their own password without a help desk ticket, but it only works for a user who has already registered qualifying authentication methods in advance — SSPR is not retroactively usable by someone who never set it up. Admins configure how many methods are required (one or two) and which method types count (Authenticator push/code, OATH hardware or software tokens, SMS, voice call, email OTP); accounts with an administrator role are always held to the stricter two-gate policy regardless of the tenant-wide setting for regular users. A subtlety worth remembering: Microsoft Authenticator alone can never satisfy a policy by itself — it must always be paired with at least one other registered method, whether the policy requires one method or two.

For hybrid environments where the user's password is actually managed on-premises (federated, PTA, or PHS-synced accounts), SSPR by itself only resets the password inside Entra ID — it has no effect on the on-premises account unless password writeback is explicitly enabled. With writeback on, an SSPR-initiated reset is pushed back down to on-premises Active Directory, so the user's AD password actually changes; without it, an on-prem-sourced user attempting SSPR is simply told to contact their administrator, since resetting only the cloud-side password would leave the two out of sync. Writeback also supports separating 'unlock the account' from 'reset the password' as two distinct user-facing options, rather than always forcing both together.

Microsoft Entra password protection layers on top of SSPR (and on top of any password change, not just self-service ones) by checking submitted passwords against a global banned-password list plus an optional custom banned-password list, and — notably — this same protection can be extended to on-premises Active Directory Domain Services via an on-prem proxy/DC agent, so weak or banned passwords get rejected at the domain controller even for changes that never touch the cloud.

title: Conditional Access: The If-Then Policy Engine
body:
Conditional Access is Microsoft Entra's Zero Trust policy engine, and its structure is deliberately simple to state even though real-world policies get complex: every policy is an if-then statement made of assignments (the "if" — who, what app, from where, on what device, under what risk level) and access controls (the "then" — what has to happen before access is granted, or whether it's blocked outright). It's important to remember Conditional Access only evaluates after first-factor authentication succeeds — it is not a substitute for a DDoS defense or a pre-authentication firewall, it's a post-authentication gate.

The assignment side pulls in signals from several independent categories that can be combined: identity (specific users, groups, or the newer agent identities for AI workloads), network location (named IP ranges, or whole country/region blocks), device platform and compliance state, target application, and real-time risk signals sourced from Microsoft Entra ID Protection (sign-in risk and user risk) plus, where licensed, Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps session signals. The control side ranges from a hard block, through grant-with-requirements (MFA, a specific authentication strength, a compliant or hybrid-joined device, an approved client app, an app protection policy, a forced password change, or terms-of-use acceptance), and policies can require several of these simultaneously.

Operationally, Conditional Access requires at least Entra ID P1 (P2 for the risk-based conditions specifically), and licenses that lapse don't auto-disable or delete existing policies — they freeze in a read-only state so an org isn't suddenly exposed by a licensing gap. For the exam, remember that admins can build policies from a blank slate or start from Microsoft's built-in policy templates, and every policy supports a report-only mode to validate its real-world impact against sign-in logs before it's switched to actually enforce.

title: Continuous Access Evaluation: Beyond Token Expiry
body:
By default, OAuth 2.0 access tokens are valid for an hour, and a client only re-checks policy when it goes back to Entra to refresh an expiring token — which means a critical event (an account getting disabled, a password reset, an admin revoking sessions) could take up to that full hour to actually take effect for an app already holding a valid token. Continuous access evaluation (CAE) closes that gap by turning the relationship between Entra and a 'CAE-aware' resource provider (initially Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams) into a two-way conversation instead of a one-way token handout: the resource provider can be told in near real time to stop honoring a token, and it can also tell Entra about a context change (like a network location shift) that needs re-evaluating.

CAE actually covers two distinct scenarios. Critical event evaluation reacts to a fixed list of high-severity events — account deletion/disable, password change/reset, MFA newly enabled, an admin's explicit revoke-all-refresh-tokens action, or Entra ID Protection detecting high user risk — and works in any tenant regardless of Conditional Access configuration. Conditional Access policy evaluation is the second, narrower scenario: it syncs IP-based location policies specifically into the resource provider itself, so a user who steps outside an allowed IP range loses access to files/email/Teams almost immediately rather than waiting for their token to expire naturally.

The practical trade-off that makes CAE worth knowing in depth: because critical events and location changes are now what drives revocation rather than a short, blunt token lifetime, CAE-aware sessions can be issued much longer-lived tokens (up to 28 hours) without weakening security — reducing the constant background refresh traffic clients would otherwise generate, while actually tightening the real-world window between a security event and its enforcement.

title: User Risk vs. Sign-In Risk in Entra ID Protection
body:
Microsoft Entra ID Protection surfaces two distinct risk signals that Conditional Access can act on, and conflating them is one of the most common exam-relevant mistakes. Sign-in risk is evaluated fresh on every individual authentication attempt — it's a real-time probability score (based on hundreds of signals) that this specific sign-in request isn't actually being made by the legitimate account owner, driven by things like anomalous travel, unfamiliar sign-in properties, or traffic from a known-malicious IP. User risk, by contrast, is a standing, cumulative assessment of the account itself — the probability that the account's credentials have been compromised at some point — built from signals like leaked-credential matches or a pattern of risky sign-ins over time, and it persists across sessions until it's explicitly remediated.

Because the two signals answer different questions, they call for different remedies. A sign-in risk policy typically responds with something that can be satisfied in the moment — block, allow, require MFA, or force reauthentication — since the concern is this one attempt. A user risk policy responds with something that addresses the standing compromise — requiring risk remediation (Entra automatically selects an appropriate flow based on the user's registered authentication methods and whether a password was actually involved), forcing a secure password change, or blocking the account outright until an admin intervenes. Both policy types are designed around self-remediation: a user who successfully completes the required control (say, a forced password change) clears their own risk state without an admin needing to manually investigate and dismiss it, which is what keeps risk-based policies operationally sustainable at scale.

A scheduling detail worth knowing: the original, separate 'risk policy' configuration surface inside Identity Protection itself is being retired (legacy risk policies stop working October 1, 2026), with all risk-based policy authoring consolidating into Conditional Access as sign-in risk and user risk conditions — which is also where the exam's current guidance points, since it unifies risk policies with the rest of an org's access-control policy set in one place.

title: Global Secure Access: Internet Access and Private Access
body:
Global Secure Access is Microsoft's umbrella term for its Security Service Edge (SSE) offering, and it's really two distinct products unified under one admin experience and delivered over Microsoft's own global network backbone. Microsoft Entra Internet Access is the identity-aware Secure Web Gateway (SWG) half — it sits between users and the open internet/SaaS apps, applying web-content-category and FQDN filtering, threat-intelligence-based blocking, and TLS inspection, while feeding rich context (user, device, location, compliance, risk) into Conditional Access so a single policy engine can govern both app access and raw network traffic together. A related, more targeted capability — Internet Access for Microsoft services — gives a client direct, optimized connectivity specifically to Microsoft's own services and enables features like Universal Tenant Restrictions and source-IP restoration for sign-in logs, without requiring the full internet-wide SWG.

Microsoft Entra Private Access is the VPN-replacement half: a Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) solution that extends the same per-app, Conditional-Access-governed model that Application Proxy pioneered for web apps out to arbitrary private TCP/UDP resources, ports, and protocols — legacy line-of-business apps, file shares, RDP/SSH targets — without publishing a broad network-level VPN tunnel. Its 'Quick Access' feature lets an admin expose a range of IPs/FQDNs without per-app configuration, useful during a phased rollout away from a legacy VPN.

Licensing-wise, both are available standalone or bundled in the Microsoft Entra Suite, and a lighter tier of Internet Access capability (the Microsoft-services-only piece) is actually included in a plain Entra ID P1/P2 license — a distinction worth remembering, since the exam may test which specific Global Secure Access capabilities are 'free' with existing Entra licensing versus which require the dedicated Internet Access or Private Access license.

title: Managed Identities for Azure Resources
body:
A managed identity is Entra's answer to the age-old problem of applications needing credentials to talk to other Azure services: instead of a developer embedding a connection string, API key, or certificate somewhere in code or configuration, Azure assigns the compute resource itself an identity that Entra ID can issue tokens for, with no secret ever exposed to the developer. There are two flavors. A system-assigned managed identity is created and destroyed along with the specific resource it's attached to (a VM, an App Service, a Function) — it's a one-to-one relationship, it can't be shared, and deleting the resource automatically deletes the identity. A user-assigned managed identity is the opposite: it's created as its own standalone Azure object with an independent lifecycle, and it can be attached to many resources at once, which makes it the better fit when several VMs or services need to share one consistent identity for accessing a downstream resource.

Behind the scenes, enabling either kind creates a special type of service principal in the tenant. That service principal is what actually gets authorized against target resources (a storage account, a Key Vault, a SQL database) via role-based access control, exactly like you'd authorize a user or an app registration. The workload then uses the Azure Identity SDK or MSAL, which transparently detects the managed identity and requests a token with no credential material the developer has to manage or rotate. A newer extension of this pattern is using a managed identity as a Federated Identity Credential (FIC) on an app registration — letting compute-hosted workloads exchange a managed identity token for an Entra app token via workload identity federation, which keeps even multi-tenant app scenarios credential-free. For the exam, the practical decision point is almost always: single resource with a private, disposable identity → system-assigned; multiple resources sharing one identity, or an identity that must outlive the resource → user-assigned.

title: Microsoft Entra Application Proxy for On-Premises Apps
body:
Application Proxy solves a specific problem: an organization has web apps that only exist on internal servers, but users need to reach them securely from outside the corporate network without a traditional VPN or a perimeter-network reverse proxy. It has two moving pieces — a cloud-hosted Application Proxy service that's part of Entra ID, and a lightweight software connector installed on a server inside the private network. Critically, the connector only makes outbound connections back to the cloud service over standard HTTPS ports, so there's no need to open any inbound firewall ports, which removes a whole category of exposure that traditional reverse proxies introduce.

The sign-in flow is worth knowing step by step for exam purposes: a user hits the app's external URL, gets redirected to Entra ID for authentication (where Conditional Access policies apply exactly as they would for a cloud SaaS app), receives a token, and that token is passed to the Application Proxy service, which extracts identity information and forwards the request to the connector. The connector then performs any additional authentication the app itself requires — Application Proxy supports Integrated Windows Authentication via Kerberos Constrained Delegation, header-based auth, form-based auth, and certificate-based scenarios — before relaying the request to the actual on-premises app and returning the response back up the chain.

The practical payoff is that once an app is published this way, end users access it exactly like any other app in their My Apps portal, with the same Conditional Access, MFA, and centralized user-lifecycle management that governs cloud apps — no code changes required in the on-premises app itself, and no exposed attack surface on the internal network beyond the outbound-only connector.

title: App Registrations, Application Objects, and Service Principals
body:
This is one of the more conceptually slippery areas of the identity platform because two closely related but distinct objects are involved. When a developer registers an app in Entra ID, that action creates an application object — a single, global definition of the app that lives in the app's "home" tenant. Think of it like a class definition in object-oriented programming: it describes how the app requests tokens, what resources it might need, and what actions it can take, but it isn't itself something that can sign in or be granted access directly.

What actually gets authorized and granted permissions in a given tenant is a service principal — a local, tenant-specific instance derived from that application object, similar to an instantiated object from a class. A single-tenant app has exactly one service principal, created automatically at registration time in its home tenant. A multitenant app can have many: one gets created in each additional tenant the moment an admin or user in that tenant consents to the app, and it's that tenant-specific service principal (not the original application object) that actually defines what the app can do and who can access it within that particular tenant. Service principals themselves come in three types: the "Application" type just described, a "Managed identity" type (created automatically for managed identities and lacking any corresponding application object), and a legacy type for pre-app-registration-era apps.

The operational implication that shows up constantly in real administration: deleting the application object in its home tenant cascades and deletes the home-tenant service principal too, but it does not touch service principals that were created in other consuming tenants — those keep functioning independently since they only inherited default properties at creation time rather than maintaining a live dependency on the application object.

title: User Consent and Admin Consent for Applications
body:
Consent is the mechanism by which an application actually gets permission to touch data on a user's or organization's behalf, expressed as the specific API permissions (delegated or application permissions) the app requests. User consent happens the first time an individual signs into an app that needs permissions they haven't already approved — they see a consent prompt describing what the app is asking for, and if they accept, that decision is recorded so they aren't re-prompted on future sign-ins to the same app for the same permissions. Whether a non-admin user is even allowed to grant this kind of consent is itself a tenant-wide setting an administrator controls, and Entra ID ships with three built-in postures: consent fully disabled for regular users, consent allowed only for apps from verified publishers requesting low-impact permissions the admin has explicitly classified, or consent allowed broadly for any permission that doesn't require admin-level approval.

Admin consent is the counterpart used when an app needs high-privilege permissions, or when an organization wants to pre-approve an app for everyone rather than making each user click through a prompt individually. A privileged admin (the specific role required depends on which permissions are being granted) can grant consent on behalf of the whole tenant in one action — after which ordinary users sign in without seeing a prompt at all, unless the app later starts requesting an additional permission the admin hasn't yet covered. Because tenant-wide admin consent can expose broad swaths of organizational data, Microsoft explicitly recommends verifying the app and its publisher's trustworthiness first, since a careless grant is functionally equivalent to handing that publisher standing access.

For situations where users aren't permitted to self-consent but still need an app, the admin consent workflow gives them a self-service request path: the user sees an "Approval required" prompt, submits a justification, and designated reviewer admins get notified to approve or deny — closing the loop without requiring the user to track down an admin manually.

title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps Overview
body:
Defender for Cloud Apps is Microsoft's cloud access security broker (CASB), built to close a visibility gap that identity and network controls alone don't cover: once a user is authenticated into a SaaS app, what are they actually doing with the data inside it, and which apps are even in use across the organization in the first place (including ones IT never sanctioned)? It works across several pillars. Cloud discovery analyzes network traffic and a large built-in app catalog to surface every SaaS app being accessed — sanctioned or not — and scores each one against more than 90 risk indicators, so administrators can see shadow IT they'd otherwise have no visibility into at all.

Beyond discovery, it layers in SaaS Security Posture Management (surfacing misconfigurations in already-connected apps and recommending fixes based on industry benchmarks), information protection (scanning connected apps for sensitive data and applying controls like sensitivity labels, download blocks to unmanaged devices, or stripping external collaborators from confidential files), and threat protection as part of Microsoft's broader XDR suite — correlating cloud-app signals with the rest of an attack chain rather than treating SaaS activity as an isolated silo.

The piece most directly relevant to workload identity governance is app-to-app protection through app governance: because OAuth-authorized apps can hold extensive delegated permissions to a user's data without much day-to-day visibility, Defender for Cloud Apps tracks both active and expired app credentials and flags apps behaving anomalously, giving admins a way to govern the sprawl of third-party OAuth apps that have quietly accumulated access over time — which is exactly the kind of blind spot that traditional identity controls alone won't catch.

title: OAuth App Policies in Defender for Cloud Apps
body:
Where cloud discovery answers "what SaaS apps are in use," OAuth app policies answer a narrower and arguably scarier question: what have users already authorized third-party apps to do with their data via OAuth, and is any of that authorization dangerous? An OAuth app policy lets an admin set conditions — for example, an app requesting a high permission level that's been authorized by more than a threshold number of users — and get automatically notified when an app matches. From there, admins can investigate exactly which permissions an app requested and which specific users granted them (across Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and Salesforce), then mark those permissions approved or banned; banning disables the enterprise application tied to that OAuth app outright.

Separate from policies an admin defines manually, Defender for Cloud Apps ships several built-in anomaly-detection policies specifically for OAuth apps, powered by machine learning and Microsoft threat intelligence rather than admin-authored rules: detecting misleading app names or misleading publisher names (a classic phishing trick using look-alike characters to impersonate a trusted app or vendor), flagging apps that get consented to under suspicious circumstances, and catching apps with anomalous file-download behavior. These anomaly detections only fire for OAuth apps actually authorized within the organization's own Entra ID tenant.

The combination matters for exam purposes because it represents defense-in-depth beyond the initial consent decision: even after a user or admin has granted an OAuth app permissions, ongoing OAuth app policies and anomaly detection give the organization a second, continuous layer of oversight over what those already-trusted apps are doing — rather than treating consent as a one-time, unmonitored decision.

title: Entitlement Management: Catalogs, Access Packages, and Access Requests
body:
Entitlement management exists to solve access sprawl at scale: as an organization grows, manually tracking who should have access to what — especially when "who" includes people outside the organization entirely — becomes unmanageable through ad hoc group additions and one-off approvals. The core building block is the access package: a bundle of everything an identity needs for a project or role, which can include membership in Entra security groups, Microsoft 365 groups and Teams, assignment to enterprise applications (including SaaS and custom-integrated apps that support SSO or provisioning), and membership in SharePoint Online sites.

Access packages live inside catalogs, which exist primarily as a delegation boundary — an admin can add any resource to any catalog, but a delegated, non-admin catalog owner can only add resources they themselves own, letting business-unit owners manage their own access packages without needing standing directory-admin rights. Each access package is governed by one or more policies, which define the actual guardrails: who's eligible to request the package (existing internal identities, or identities from specific external connected organizations), what approval workflow applies, and how long an approved assignment lasts before it automatically expires and must be renewed.

The request lifecycle itself follows a predictable shape: an eligible identity submits an access request against a package, it routes through whatever approval workflow the policy defines, and on approval the requester receives a time-limited assignment. This time-limited-by-default design is deliberate — it directly counters the common failure mode where access, once granted, is never revisited, since entitlement management pairs naturally with recurring access reviews to keep assignments honest over time rather than accumulating indefinitely.

title: Terms of Use and Connected Organizations
body:
Terms of use (ToU) policies solve a compliance need distinct from access control itself: before a user is allowed into a resource, the organization needs proof they actually saw and accepted a specific document — an acceptable-use policy, a data-handling agreement, whatever legal or compliance requires. A ToU policy is built around an uploaded PDF (localizable into multiple language versions, with the version shown chosen by the user's browser language) and is enforced through a Conditional Access policy, meaning it can be scoped as tightly as a single app or as broadly as every user in the tenant. Administrators can require re-acceptance on a recurring schedule or after a fixed number of days, and every acceptance or decline is logged and reportable — a user who declines is simply blocked from the resource until they sign back in and accept.

Connected organizations solve a different, but related, governance problem: giving entitlement management a durable way to recognize which external organization a guest access requester actually belongs to, so access packages can be scoped to "anyone from Contoso" rather than manually vetting every external individual one at a time. A connected organization can be defined against another Entra tenant, a non-Microsoft directory using SAML/WS-Fed federation, a plain email domain (verified via one-time passcode for organizations with no formal identity federation at all), or even personal Microsoft accounts for cases with no organizational affiliation whatsoever. Connected organizations carry a state — configured (deliberately set up and fully trusted by an admin) versus proposed (auto-created the moment an unrecognized external user successfully requests access, sitting in a kind of unverified holding state) — and that distinction matters operationally, because access-package policies that say "allow all configured connected organizations" deliberately exclude the proposed ones until an admin reviews and promotes them.

title: Access Reviews: Planning, Creating, Monitoring, and Responding
body:
Access reviews exist to answer a question that self-service access models constantly create: once someone has access — whether through a group, an app assignment, a privileged role, or an entitlement-management package — does that access still make sense, or has it just been sitting there unexamined since the day it was granted? Rather than being one single feature, access reviews are really an evaluation capability that plugs into several different underlying access mechanisms, and where a review actually gets created depends on what's being reviewed: reviews of security-group or Microsoft 365 group membership and of app assignments are created directly in access reviews or the Entra enterprise apps blade, reviews of Entra directory roles or Azure resource roles are created inside Privileged Identity Management, and reviews of access-package assignments are created inside entitlement management itself.

A handful of situations make access reviews the right tool specifically: recertifying who holds privileged roles like Global Administrator (including catching guest or partner accounts that never got cleaned up after a one-off task), covering gaps where automation can't reach — dynamic-membership rules work fine when the underlying HR attribute exists in Entra, but they can't account for someone who still legitimately needs access after leaving a group to train a replacement — reconfirming access before repurposing a group for a new, more sensitive context, and maintaining a defensible, auditable record of any policy exceptions an organization has had to grant.

Once a review is running, reviewers (who can be specifically designated people, resource owners, or the users themselves in a self-review) get notified at the start of each cycle and approve or deny continued access through a dedicated access panel, aided by system-generated recommendations. Reviews can be configured to recur automatically on a set cadence — weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annually — which is what turns access reviews from a one-time cleanup exercise into an ongoing governance control rather than a project that quietly stops happening after the first pass.

title: Privileged Identity Management for Entra Roles and Azure Resource Roles
body:
PIM exists to eliminate the standing-privileged-account problem: instead of a person holding Global Administrator (or any sensitive Entra or Azure resource role) permanently and constantly, PIM lets an org grant just-in-time, time-bound access that's only "live" when someone actually needs it and can be tied to approval and MFA requirements. The core distinction to internalize is eligible versus active. An active assignment grants the role's privileges immediately with no extra action required — functionally identical to a traditional standing assignment. An eligible assignment grants nothing by default; the user must first activate it, which can involve completing an MFA challenge, typing a business justification, and (if the role requires it) waiting on a designated approver to sign off before the privileges actually apply for a bounded window of time.

Who can administer this differs depending on what's being managed: for Entra roles, only Privileged Role Administrators or Global Administrators can manage other admins' assignments, while for Azure resource roles it's subscription owners, resource owners, or User Access Administrators — meaning PIM effectively straddles two separate permission models depending on which resource type is in scope, which is a detail worth remembering since it's an easy point of confusion.

Once assignments exist, the operational loop is: assign (an admin sets eligible or active status, scope, and duration) → activate (the eligible user performs whatever actions the role requires to go live) → approve or deny (if the role requires approval, a designated approver acts on the request) → extend or renew (as an assignment nears or passes its expiration, the affected user can request more time, itself subject to approval). Throughout, PIM enforces guardrails like preventing removal of the very last active Global Administrator, and it retains a full activation/approval audit history for internal or external audit purposes.

title: PIM for Groups and Break-Glass Emergency Access Accounts
body:
PIM for Groups extends the same just-in-time model used for Entra and Azure resource roles to group membership and ownership itself. Rather than making a user eligible for a specific role directly, an admin can make a Microsoft Entra security group or Microsoft 365 group PIM-eligible, so users activate temporary membership or ownership in that group — and because groups are commonly used to control access to Entra roles, Azure roles, Key Vault, Intune, and countless application roles, this becomes a flexible way to grant just-in-time access to a whole bundle of downstream permissions through one activation rather than juggling many separate eligible role assignments. Each PIM-for-Groups-enabled group carries two independent policies, one governing membership activation and one governing ownership activation, and one wrinkle worth remembering: role-assignable groups (the special group type that can itself be assigned an Entra role) can't have other groups nested inside them, which limits how deeply you can chain group-based eligibility.

Break-glass, or emergency access, accounts solve a completely different but equally critical problem: what happens if every legitimate path to admin access breaks simultaneously — a federation provider outage, every admin's MFA device unreachable during a natural disaster, or the departure of the last Global Administrator? The guidance is to maintain at least two dedicated, cloud-only accounts (never federated or synced from on-premises, so they can't be taken down by the same outage that locks everyone else out), secured with a phishing-resistant method like a FIDO2 key that's deliberately different from what regular admin accounts use, and explicitly excluded from Conditional Access policies that could block sign-in — since a policy that requires the very thing that's unavailable during the emergency defeats the account's entire purpose. Their Global Administrator role assignment should be permanent and active in PIM (not eligible, since activation itself might depend on infrastructure that's down), and organizations are expected to monitor every sign-in to these accounts with alerting and to validate they still work through regular drills, typically at least every 90 days.

title: Monitoring Identity Activity: Logs, Diagnostic Settings, KQL, and Secure Score
body:
Entra ID's monitoring story is built on three distinct activity-log types, and knowing which one answers which kind of question is genuinely useful, not just trivia: audit logs record the history of every administrative task performed in the tenant (who changed a role assignment, who modified an app's configuration), sign-in logs capture every sign-in attempt from users and client applications (revealing sign-in patterns, volume trends, and which clients are authenticating against which apps), and provisioning logs track identities being created, updated, or removed in the tenant through a third-party provisioning connector (confirming, for instance, that a user removal in an HR system actually propagated through to a downstream SaaS app).

These logs are viewable directly in the admin center or via Microsoft Graph, but for any kind of long-term retention or serious analysis they need to be routed out to a destination through diagnostic settings — the standard options being an Azure Monitor Log Analytics workspace (for querying with Kusto Query Language and building workbooks), a storage account (for cheap long-term archival), or an Azure Event Hub (typically used to stream logs onward into a third-party SIEM). KQL is the query language used against Log Analytics — the practical pattern is filtering a table like SigninLogs or AuditLogs down by a condition (a specific user's object ID, a result type, a time window) and projecting just the columns that matter, which is exactly the kind of query an admin writes to investigate a specific suspicious sign-in or to build a recurring alert rule.

On top of raw log access, Entra layers purpose-built reporting: Identity Protection turns sign-in data into risky-user and risky-sign-in reports, Microsoft Entra workbooks provide prebuilt customizable visualizations over the same log data, and Identity Secure Score gives a single aggregated, actionable number reflecting how well the tenant's current configuration aligns with Microsoft's security recommendations — functioning as a running scorecard admins can use to prioritize which governance and security gaps to close next, rather than treating monitoring as purely reactive incident investigation.
